One equation, ten schemes

CFD 4 · linear advection

∂u/∂t + a ∂u/∂x = 0 u(x,t) = u₀(x − at)
Grid & time-step details

Periodic domain [−1, 1), with no duplicate endpoint. Both schemes use exactly the same grid and time step Δt = |C| Δx / |a|. Changing a numerical setting restarts at t = 0. The time step is never reduced to stabilize a scheme.

Initial-condition formula
Edit the shared initial curve
How this curve is used

Both schemes sample this same curve on the selected grid. Editing the curve restarts both at t = 0; changing the grid resamples the same curve. The dashed exact solution translates this curve continuously. Curve settings are remembered for this site address when local storage is available.

Numerical errors and solution ranges
SchemeL₂ errorL∞ errorMin / maxMass drift
How to read the results

Errors compare node values with the exact solution at the same physical time: L₂ = √(Σ|uᵢ − uexact(xᵢ,t)|² / N), L∞ = max|error|. Mass drift is |Δx Σuᵢ − Δx Σuᵢ⁰|. Discontinuities limit convergence and may generate overshoots. A stable method can still be inaccurate.

Follow one time step

  1. Read the current fieldChoose uⁿ and wrap neighboring indices across periodic boundaries.
  2. Apply the selected difference formulaExplicit schemes update from known values; implicit schemes solve the periodic coupled system.
  3. Move to the next time levelBoth schemes use the same Δt. Leapfrog retains the previous level; CIP also transports the derivative.
  4. Compare with exact transportTranslate the initial profile by at, then measure error, overshoot and mass drift.

Difference formulas & stability

∂u∂t+a∂u∂x=0C=aΔtΔx
Notation & assumptions

Formulas below use signed C = aΔt/Δx. Here r = |C| and s = sign(a), so upstream stencils follow the velocity direction. Stability statements apply to constant-speed linear advection on a uniform periodic grid. Formal orders assume a smooth solution and fixed nonzero CFL.

Stability reference

The stability summaries supplement the handout with Fourier analysis for the periodic, constant-coefficient problem. They describe linear stability, not monotonicity or accuracy.
